newsitem.title: INDIA: Nepal 1997 real GDP growth seen at 4.5 pct vs 6.1.
newsitem.headline: Nepal 1997 real GDP growth seen at 4.5 pct vs 6.1.

text.p: The Himalayan kingdom of Nepal is expected to post real GDP growth of 4.5 percent in the year ending on July 15, 1997, rising to 5.0 percent in 1998, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.
In a country report, ADB said real gross domestic product growth was 6.1 percent in 1996, up from 2.9 percent in 1995.
ADB said the increase in real GDP growth in 1996 was broad-based.

"A good monsoon helped lift agricultural output by 5.4 percent. The industry sector grew by 5.3 percent, stimulated by a revival in the production of carpets and garments - the main exports of the country," the ADB report said.
Liberalisation of the trade regime, improvement in customs valuation and unification of the exchange rate also contributed to a significant rationalisation of industrial incentives, the report said.

The ADB said Nepal faced formidable challenges -- ensuring macroeconomic stability, stability of its external account, fostering a dynamic private sector and strengthening the efficiency of its public (state-run firms) sector.
ADB said growth in agricultural productivity was essential for overall economic performance.
"Agricultural growth was favourable in 1996, a break from the recent trend, but it needs to be sustained. It averaged only 2.7 percent a year during 1990-1995," ADB said.
The government's inability to supply adequate fertilisers on a timely basis has been a drag on agricultural growth, it said.
ADB said industrial GDP was estimated to grow by 5.7 percent and 7.7 percent in 1997 and 1998, respectively.
Rising tourist arrivals and increasing trading and financial activity will underpin growth of the services sector, it said.
"Improved economic performance in the near term assumes good weather, the beginning of implementation of the agriculture perspective plan and revitalisation of reform efforts," the ADB report said.
"Nevertheless, with investment growing faster than saving, difficulties in funding the widening resource gap may constrain development," the bank warned.
